passage:
I'm Deepak. In Class 6 science, Elizabeth ma'am was explaining rainbows and I asked, "But why are the colours always in the same order?" She sighed. "Don't ask silly questions, Deepak. Stick to the book." A few people laughed. My face went hot.
After that I kept my hand down. I still wondered about things, like why ink spreads in water and why the moon has days, but I wrote them in the back of my notebook instead. I stopped asking anyone. Sometimes, when I see a rainbow, the question comes back and sits with me.

qa.q: What did Deepak ask about rainbows?
qa.a: Deepak asked why the colours are always in the same order.

qa.q: What did Deepak feel when Elizabeth ma'am said not to ask silly questions?
qa.a: Deepak felt embarrassed and ashamed, with a hot face, and stopped raising a hand.

qa.q: What could a teacher do so that a student like Deepak keeps asking?
qa.a: A teacher could welcome the question, or say it is a good one and give a moment for it later. A question box could also give a safe place.

qa.q: How might the classmates who laughed have seen the moment?
qa.a: They may have followed the teacher's tone and thought the question was silly, without realising how it landed on Deepak.

grounding: A child told not to ask silly questions stops asking, though the curiosity persists privately.

passage:
Note by Bhupen, class teacher, Class 5.
Binita used to ask a question in every lesson. A month ago another teacher told her in front of the class, "Don't ask silly questions." Since then she has not raised her hand once, though she still studies the wall charts and scribbles on the last page of her notebook.
I have put a question box on my desk. Yesterday I found a folded slip: "Why do stars look small but are big?" I answered it aloud without naming anyone. This morning Binita lifted her hand for the first time in weeks. I will keep the box open, and I will keep answering.
— Bhupen

qa.q: Where did Bhupen put the question box?
qa.a: Bhupen put the question box on the desk.

qa.q: What did Binita probably feel when told not to ask silly questions in front of the class?
qa.a: Binita likely felt embarrassed and discouraged, and stopped raising her hand, while the curiosity carried on privately.

qa.q: What did Bhupen do that made it safe for Binita to ask again?
qa.a: Bhupen offered a question box, answered a slip aloud without naming anyone, and kept it open. That let Binita ask without being exposed.

qa.q: How does Bhupen read Binita's silence?
qa.a: Bhupen sees it as curiosity dampened, not gone, since Binita still studies the charts and writes in the notebook.

grounding: A child who is told not to ask silly questions stops asking; a teacher creates a safe way to bring the questions back.

passage: In the Class 3 science period at her school in Jalandhar, Gurleen put her hand up for the third time. "Ma'am, why do onions make us cry?" A few kids giggled. The teacher sighed. "Gurleen, don't ask silly questions. Just learn what's in the book." Gurleen put her hand down fast. For the rest of the week she didn't raise it once, even when she knew the answers. Her friend Himani noticed. "You're so quiet now." "Questions are silly," Gurleen said, shrugging. But at home that night, she opened a small notebook with a sparkly cover and wrote, "Why do onions make us cry? Why are some leaves red? Why do cats purr?" She hid it under her mattress.

qa.q: Where did Gurleen hide her notebook?
qa.a: Under her mattress.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling when she put her hand down fast?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and hurt, as if her curiosity was unwelcome in class.

qa.q: How could the teacher respond differently to Gurleen's question?
qa.a: The teacher could say, 'Good question, let's find out,' or suggest looking it up together after class.

qa.q: How does Himani notice the change in Gurleen?
qa.a: Himani sees that Gurleen has become quiet, and may feel puzzled or sad about it.

grounding: Shows a child told not to ask silly questions who stops asking in class while her curiosity continues privately.

passage:
"Sir, why don't we fall off the Earth if it's round?"
"Omkar, we're doing multiplication tables. Don't ask silly questions."
Some kids laughed. Omkar sat down.
At break, Zeenat found him by the water tank.
"That was a good question," she said.
"No, it was silly. Sir said."
"I wanted to know too."
Omkar shrugged. "I'm not asking anything anymore."
"Not even in science?"
"Not anywhere." He kicked the tank.
"My Abbu says it's gravity. Like a magnet, sort of."
Omkar looked up, eyes lighting for a second. "Really? Like a magnet?"
Then he looked away. "Doesn't matter."
"It does to me," said Zeenat. "Ask me next time."

qa.q: What subject was the class doing when Omkar asked his question?
qa.a: Multiplication tables.

qa.q: What shows that Omkar still felt curious after being dismissed?
qa.a: His eyes lit up when Zeenat mentioned gravity, before he looked away and said it didn't matter.

qa.q: How could Zeenat keep supporting Omkar's curiosity?
qa.a: She could keep sharing answers and questions with him, and maybe suggest asking the science teacher together.

qa.q: What would change if Sir had said 'Good question, let's talk about it later'?
qa.a: Omkar might have felt his wondering was welcome and kept asking questions in class.

grounding: Shows a child told not to ask silly questions who stops asking, though his curiosity still flickers privately.

passage:
When I was in Class 4, I asked Minakshi ma'am at tuition why volcanoes erupt. She said, "Tarun, don't waste time with silly questions. Finish your sums." Everyone was quiet.
After that, I stopped asking. At tuition, then at school. It felt safer to just copy what was on the board.
For a while, I stopped wondering, too. I didn't even notice.
Then last month, at the library, I found a book about volcanoes. I read it standing up, all of it. My heart was thumping. I hadn't felt like that in so long.
I still don't ask much in class. But I keep a list of questions on my phone now, and I read about one every night.

qa.q: What did Tarun ask Minakshi ma'am at tuition?
qa.a: Why volcanoes erupt.

qa.q: How did Tarun feel reading the volcano book at the library?
qa.a: Tarun felt excited and alive, heart thumping, as if a long-lost curiosity had come back.

qa.q: What could a teacher do to help Tarun ask questions again?
qa.a: A teacher could welcome Tarun's questions openly, maybe inviting Tarun to share one from the phone list with the class.

qa.q: What was it like for the other children when Minakshi ma'am dismissed Tarun?
qa.a: Everyone went quiet, so they may have learned too that questions were not welcome.

grounding: Shows a child who stops asking after a dismissive reply, whose curiosity fades for a while before quietly returning.

passage:
Tuition notes: Baljeet, Class 4, after six weeks.
In our first sessions Baljeet asked something every few minutes: why fractions get smaller when the bottom number grows, why ants walk in lines. For two weeks now, almost nothing. Today I asked why. Baljeet shrugged, then said, "Suraj Sir said in science to stop asking silly questions and let him finish the chapter. Everyone laughed." Since then Baljeet has been writing questions in the back of a rough notebook instead. There were eleven, including "Do fish sleep?" We spent the last ten minutes on three of them. I told Baljeet those are exactly the kind of questions scientists ask. I will also speak calmly to Suraj Sir at the parents' meeting on Saturday about what I have seen.

qa.q: How many questions were in the back of Baljeet's rough notebook?
qa.a: There were eleven.

qa.q: What was Baljeet feeling after the class laughed?
qa.a: Baljeet likely felt embarrassed and ashamed of asking, so the questions went into a hidden notebook instead.

qa.q: What did the tutor do that could bring the questions back?
qa.a: Spending time on three of them and calling them scientists' questions showed Baljeet that wondering is welcome.

qa.q: How might Suraj Sir see that moment in science class?
qa.a: Suraj Sir may have seen it as keeping the chapter on track, not realising the remark taught Baljeet to stop asking.

grounding: Shows a child who was told to stop asking silly questions going quiet in class while the curiosity survives privately.
